# Which material changes can two spectra identify? {#sec-identifiability}

## Motivation

Dual-energy CT measures each ray at two spectra, but we want three tissue fractions per pixel: adipose, fibroglandular
tissue and calcification. Two measurements cannot determine three unknowns without extra information. Before asking whether
any learned method can recover the three maps, we need to know *which* combinations of changes the measurements can see at
all, and how fragile the recovery is once a constraint such as "the fractions sum to one" is added.

## Formulation

In each pixel the measurement is a linear map of the fractions, $\mathbf{y}=A\mathbf{x}$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times3}$
(@eq-linear). Any $\mathbf{n}$ in the null space of $A$ satisfies $A(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n})=A\mathbf{x}$ and is invisible to
the data. Appending the row $\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}=1$ gives a square matrix $B$ whose conditioning controls how
measurement error is amplified in the estimate. This is the image-domain model; the benchmark's data were generated by the
polychromatic model of @eq-beer, and the images used below, which the records describe as reconstructed from those data by filtered back-projection (a standard reconstruction step), are therefore not exactly described by the linear model.

## What the numbers say

[Computed from the official starting-kit spectra and attenuation tables at zero path length, the spectrum-averaged attenuation matrix is $A\approx\begin{pmatrix}0.267&0.313&3.012\\0.219&0.248&1.642\end{pmatrix}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$, with rows the 50 and 80 kVp spectra and columns adipose, fibroglandular tissue and calcification.]{#clm-0076 .claim} (The angle, condition number and amplification factor quoted below were computed from the unrounded entries; the three-decimal values displayed here are rounded and, because the second singular value is tiny, do not reproduce them exactly.) Calcification stands apart (its column is large and points in a different direction), whereas the first two columns are nearly proportional.

[Adipose and fibroglandular tissue are spectrally almost degenerate: their effective attenuation columns differ by only
about 1.04 degrees, so a change that trades one against the other barely alters the two measurements.]{#clm-0001 .claim} The
angle is that between the two columns of $A$ at zero path length (it falls to roughly 0.87-0.97 degrees as the beam hardens). The
null direction of $A$ is therefore dominated by exactly this exchange, compensated jointly by a small calcification change and a larger change in the total tissue fraction (@sec-theory).

[With the sum-to-one constraint the three-material problem is formally unique, but measurement error in the worst
direction is amplified by a factor of about 343; the zero-thickness condition number of the augmented matrix (about 1273)
is an upper bound on its beam-hardened value.]{#clm-0002 .claim} Beam hardening changes the effective attenuation with path
length, so the operative conditioning differs from the zero-thickness value.

## Two regimes in the benchmark phantoms

The sum-to-one constraint is only as good as the assumption that every pixel is entirely tissue. The benchmark phantoms break this, and the way the records describe the break was itself corrected.

[Over the ten starting-kit sample cases the three fraction maps sum to zero in about 35% of pixels (air background, with no fourth material class), and to one in the bulk of the remaining pixels; a boundary band of partial-volume pixels, whose sum lies strictly between zero and one, accounts for the rest.]{#clm-0077 .claim} The size of that band depends on the tolerance used to decide that "the sum equals one": [with strict equality the split is air 35.1%, tissue 51.1% and boundary band 13.8%, whereas with a tolerance of $10^{-3}$ it is air 36.3%, tissue 60.4% and band 3.4%.]{#clm-0078 .claim} Any statement about "the boundary fraction" must therefore name its tolerance. [All ten kit cases have an identical support mask, so the regime split is one observation repeated ten times rather than ten independent confirmations.]{#clm-0079 .claim} These are the ten sample cases of the starting kit, not the thousand-case training set, which had not been downloaded when the counts were made. The counts were verified interactively and were not registered as run metrics.

[We first described the phantoms as 35% air, 60% tissue and about 5% boundary, using a calcification maximum of 0.566 as a ten-case figure and treating the ten cases as independent confirmations; later checking showed that 0.566 belongs to the first case alone (the ten-case maximum is 0.738), that the cases share one mask, and that the boundary fraction moves by a factor of four with the tolerance.]{#clm-0080 .claim} What stood unchanged is the two-regime structure itself.

Two consequences follow, and they have to be kept distinct. First, [the sum-to-one constraint is valid on tissue pixels only: it is false in air, where the fractions sum to zero, and in boundary pixels, where it contradicts the measurement and the contradiction is amplified by the poor conditioning of $B$, so the resulting error far exceeds the deficit $1-\sum_j x_j$ itself.]{#clm-0081 .claim} Second, deciding which pixels are air is a modelling choice and is not recoverable from the data alone. [The classical estimators declare a pixel air, and set all three fractions to zero, when both reconstructed attenuations fall below $0.1\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$, about half the smallest tissue attenuation; this cutoff is a modelling choice that the records describe as untested on real data, and the real-image runs below used it unchanged.]{#clm-0082 .claim} If the cutoff coincided with the true air mask, air pixels would be zeroed correctly and would contribute exactly zero error, diluting all-pixel error measures. No record reports how well the cutoff matches the true air mask, however, and boundary pixels whose attenuation falls below the cutoff are zeroed too, so this was not checked.

On synthetic benchmark-style data the boundary band dominated. [On 17 noiseless synthetic validation cases (32 by 32 pixels, with the real attenuation tables), the sum-to-one estimator recovered tissue pixels almost exactly (RMSE $1.3\times10^{-6}$) yet scored 1.179 by the benchmark's primary score (a per-case root-mean-square error averaged over cases, a different statistic from the pooled-pixel RMSE used for the real images below), worse than predicting zero (0.430), because the boundary band had RMSE 3.84; the simplex estimator, which merely clips the same outliers, scored 0.051.]{#clm-0083 .claim} The surviving general lesson concerns metric design: a pooled error over a multi-regime phantom is dominated by its most mis-modelled population and can rank a clipped estimator above an exact one, so errors have to be reported by regime. That synthetic finding was later superseded by a scope correction that restricts it to synthetic data, and it is told that way here. The specific ordering did not transfer to real images (below): the synthetic band is 9.5% of pixels against 3.4% to 13.8% on the kit depending on tolerance, and on the real images tissue pixels fail worst.

An earlier design decision had framed the benchmark differently. [We first treated the benchmark as an exact-recovery problem: because the data are noiseless and the forward model is shared with all participants, the sum-to-one constraint (two measurements plus one partition equation) was expected to make the three-material problem well posed, with nonnegativity and priors judged unnecessary, and the published winning error of order $10^{-6}$ (taken from the challenge report; not independently verified here) was read as reachable by exact inversion.]{#clm-0084 .claim} The real-image results below show that this holds only where the model that justifies the constraint is exact.

## A correction to our earlier understanding

[We first believed that, because the benchmark data are noiseless, exact recovery with the sum-to-one constraint was
possible.]{#clm-0003 .claim} That belief rested on synthetic data generated with the very linear model that was then inverted,
so it demonstrated only self-consistency. It should not be read as a current conclusion.

The test was then repeated on *official benchmark images*: images the benchmark organisers reconstructed from their
simulated phantoms (not scanner or patient data). [On official benchmark tissue pixels the linear effective-attenuation
model misfits the reconstructed images by about 7.8% at 50 kVp and 5.9% at 80 kVp.]{#clm-0005 .claim} Amplified by the factor
above, this misfit is large enough to account for the failure described next, though a controlled test of that cause was not
run.

Four estimators are compared (the figure adds a fifth, the clipped sum-to-one); each sets pixels it declares air to zero. *Predicting zero* is the trivial reference. *Unconstrained* inverts $A$ per pixel with the
minimum-norm solution. *Sum-to-one* inverts $B$. *Simplex* projects the sum-to-one solution onto fractions that are
nonnegative and sum to one. [On three official benchmark images (all-pixel RMSE, about 35% of pixels air, which the estimators zero) the unclipped sum-to-one
estimator is worse than predicting zero (RMSE 1.555 against 0.447), while the unconstrained and simplex estimators are better
(0.317 and 0.379).]{#clm-0004 .claim} @fig-real-kit-rmse shows
the comparison. [Restricted to tissue pixels (fractions summing to one within $10^{-3}$) the log of the retrospective verification run gives 1.749 for sum-to-one against 0.568 for predicting zero, with unconstrained 0.404 and simplex 0.474; the written finding quotes 1.823 and 0.567 for the first pair, and the cause of that disagreement (perhaps a different tissue mask) is unresolved, so only the run-log values are used here.]{#clm-0085 .claim} If the air cutoff is right (not checked), most of the large error comes from tissue pixels rather than from air. Rough arithmetic, combining the ten-case tissue share of about 60% with the three-image RMSEs (so a mixed estimate), attributes roughly three quarters of the squared all-pixel error to tissue pixels and leaves about a quarter to boundary-band pixels and any misclassified air. On real images tissue pixels therefore fail worst, though not by themselves, and the unconstrained estimator is best.

Horizontal axis: RMSE in volume-fraction units (dimensionless); one bar is the trivial reference of predicting zero (0.447). Bars are point values from a single evaluation (no uncertainty interval is available), and the three images share
one support mask. The unclipped sum-to-one estimator, in red (1.555), is more than three times the error of predicting
zero (0.447).](../figures/real-kit-rmse.svg){#fig-real-kit-rmse fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of volume-fraction RMSE for five estimators (including a predict-zero reference) on three official benchmark images. The unclipped sum-to-one bar (1.555) is the longest and exceeds the predict-zero bar (0.447); the unconstrained (0.317), simplex (0.379) and clipped sum-to-one (0.379) bars are shorter than predict-zero."}

The simplex estimator's apparent advantage over predicting zero deserves a caution: [imposing the simplex constraint by
projection gives the same error as clipping the sum-to-one solution to the interval 0 to 1 (0.3787 against 0.3789), and 43.9% of the
sum-to-one pixels fall outside the physical range, so the apparent advantage of the simplex estimator over predicting zero
comes from clipping outliers, not from the constraint (the largest unclipped value was 23.6 where the physical range is 0 to 1).]{#clm-0063 .claim}

## Interpretation and limits

The ordering in @fig-real-kit-rmse is consistent with the amplification argument: an estimator that inverts an inexact
linear model through an ill-conditioned matrix magnifies the model error, while estimators that do not invert it exactly stay
closer to a small-error solution. This is an **interpretation**; the comparison does not isolate the cause. Three images
with one shared support mask are few, and the evidence behind the correction has not been independently reviewed, so the
conclusion is preliminary. A comparison on 100 validation cases points the same way (@sec-labelfree).

## What remains open

Whether any prior or additional information can select the adipose/fibroglandular split without labels is the subject of
the later investigations.
